Mollâ Sadrâ's struggle continues the work of Haydar Âmolî. “Tradition” involves handing down the spiritual trust to its rightful heir, who alone can receive it—but only by undergoing a new birth. Ma'qul and manqûl (rational philosophy and theology grounded in transmitted authority) still belong to the outward domain, dependent upon a chain of purely human intermediaries. Only the esoteric sciences ('olûm al-bâtin) are passed on through spiritual inheritance ('olûm irthîya), and this transmission does not happen simply “in the course of history.” It depends on an unveiling or direct insight (kashf) whose source lies in another dimension: the Malakût, the spiritual world. That is what Mollâ Sadrâ's opponents cannot understand. ↩

Commentary on § 5. We should recall here what Suhrawardi means by 'ilm hozûrî (hodûrî): knowledge that arises not through a form representing its object, but as direct insight, effective presence—“knowledge by presence.” The human being is not in time, still less a person “of his time.” Time is the measure or quantity of his very being. In the subtle state of the Malakût, that measure stretches out across pasts and futures, arranged together in the simultaneity of a spatial order that dense, material time (kathîf) can perceive only as succession. When time folds inward, an absolute presence arises—that is, a presence free from the conditions of dense time. Events of this world are no longer seen in their material, sensory condition, as successive happenings in dense time, but in their malakûtî condition, established in their proper places within the space of the Malakût. ↩
